title: The small things
hook: the Buddha refrains from even small unkindness, like idle talk and shows
carry: the ground the summit stands on

segments.voice: Yesterday: vanna and avanna on the road, and your line, not elated, not angry. What was true in the praise or blame you met? Today, what people actually praise the Buddha for. Day five hundred twenty-four.

Board games on eight-row and ten-row boards. Games played on imaginary boards in the air. Dice. Toy plows and toy windmills. Guessing what a friend is thinking. Elephant fights, ballad singers, acrobats. This is a real list, from the first long discourse, and it's a snapshot of what people did for fun long ago. It's there because the Buddha is describing what he doesn't do. And, he says, these little things are what an ordinary person praises him for. Today: the small things.
screen: `DICE, BOARD GAMES, ELEPHANT FIGHTS.` → `A SNAPSHOT OF ANCIENT FUN.` → `WHAT PEOPLE PRAISE HIM FOR.`

segments.voice: After yesterday's teaching on vanna and avanna, the Buddha says something surprising. When an ordinary person praises me, he tells the monks, it's for small matters, mere moral conduct. Then he lists them. He's put down the stick and the sword. He's gentle and kind, compassionate toward all living beings. He takes only what's given. He speaks the truth, he's reliable. He doesn't carry tales from one group to another to split them apart. He brings together those who are divided, and he enjoys harmony. His speech isn't harsh. It's pleasant to the ear, it goes to the heart. He doesn't waste words. He speaks at the right time, about what's true and useful. Then the finer points. He doesn't damage seeds or plants. He doesn't go to shows: dancing, singing, music, those elephant fights. He doesn't play the games. He doesn't trade in false weights and measures. He doesn't pass the day in what the text calls low talk: talk of kings and robbers, food and clothes, gossip at the well. The Pali word for all this is sila: moral conduct, virtue. And here's the twist. The Buddha calls it small. The real teaching, he says, is deeper, and the rest of the discourse goes there. But notice that he practices every one of the small things anyway. The small things aren't the summit. They're the ground the summit stands on. Kind speech, no gossip, careful hands. The list is long, and almost every item is small enough to do today.
screen: `WHAT ORDINARY PEOPLE PRAISE` · `NO STICK, NO SWORD, NO TALE-BEARING` · `NO SHOWS, NO GAMES, NO LOW TALK` · `SMALL, BUT THE GROUND OF IT ALL` · then, large: `THE SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refine one small habit. Go through the list slowly in your mind. Gentle speech. No carrying tales. Speaking at the right time. Not wasting words. Taking only what's given. Let one of them light up, the one closest to your actual life. Picture the moment today when it will come up. See yourself doing the small thing a little better. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sila. Moral conduct, virtue, in its smallest forms: kind speech, no gossip, careful hands. Small, and still practiced. Today's word.
Your line: the ground the summit stands on. Today, when a bit of gossip starts, don't carry it on to the next person. Day five hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists keep five precepts, and in Theravada communities some take eight on observance days, which add refraining from entertainments, adornment and luxurious beds: a lay echo of the conduct listed in DN 1.

fork.setup: two groups of friends have fallen out, and you've heard what each says about the other. according to DN 1's list, what does the Buddha do in this spot?
options: brings divided people together and enjoys harmony.
repeats each side's words to the other.
fork.reveal: he doesn't carry tales from one group to another to split them; he brings together those who are divided.

original.note: Pali sila (Sanskrit shila): moral conduct, virtue, the ground of practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: small things don't matter much in a spiritual life.
what it means: the Buddha calls them small but practices every one, as the ground of everything else.
what a scholar hears: the morality sections (short, middle, long) recur in all thirteen opening discourses of the Digha, which is why the first division is called the Silakkhandha Vagga.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta, the sections on moral conduct

notes: DN 1 paraphrased. Confirm the listed items (games on eight- and ten-row boards, games on imaginary boards, dice, toy plows and windmills, guessing thoughts, elephant fights, false weights, 'low talk' topics including gossip at the well).
Confirm the framing that ordinary people praise the Tathagata only for trifling matters of moral conduct.
The eight precepts on observance days (howItsDone) are standard Theravada lay practice; confirm.

Editor review: cut the unsourced 'two and a half thousand years' and 'most people' (the text says an ordinary person praises the Tathagata for these); replaced 'trembling for' with a plainer paraphrase; eight precepts tied to Theravada practice.
